signals.title: fix(desktop): preserve multi-pane plugins when closing panes
signals.text: ## What & why Closing a pane contributed by a plugin previously disabled the **entire plugin**, unloading every one of its contributions. For a plugin that owns several independent panes — e.g. Bot Mode's Cronjobs pane alongside its Bots roster and composer middleware — closing one pane silently killed the rest. Now, closing a pane from a multi-pane plugin **dismisses only that pane**: the plugin stays enabled and its other panes, commands, and middleware keep working. **Reset layout** restores dismissed contributed panes. A single-pane plugin keeps the existing symmetric behavior (Close disables the plugin, with **Settings → Plugins** as the discoverable recovery path). ## How to test 1. Install a multi-pane plugin (e.g. Hermes-Bot-Mode) and open two of its panes. 2. Close one pane (e.g. Cronjobs) — it disappears; the plugin's other pane (Bots roster) stays functional. 3. Confirm the plugin is still enabled in **Settings → Plugins**. 4. Reset layout — the dismissed pane returns. 5. Single-pane plugin: closing its only pane still disables the plugin. Regression coverage: `apps/desktop/src/components/pane-shell/tree/plugin-pane-close.test.ts` (multi-pane dismiss, dismissal surviving pane adoption, single-pane disable). ## Platforms tested - Linux desktop UI test suite: 3,829 tests passed (426 files), ESLint clean. ## Related No related issue — reported directly from the Hermes-Bot-Mode plugin user experience.

signals.title: fix(tools): insert -- end-of-options separator before search_files patterns
signals.text: Fixes #85795. ## Problem `_search_with_rg` and `_search_with_grep` built their shell commands without the `--` end-of-options separator before the pattern argument. `_escape_shell_arg` correctly single-quotes the pattern (a shell word-splitting concern), but that does nothing to stop `rg`/`grep` themselves from parsing a leading `-` as an option flag. Any pattern starting with `-` (the extremely common Markdown checkbox `- [ ]`, diff-style lines like `-foo`, etc.) failed silently -- `total_count: 0` with an error string a cron job never surfaces. ## Fix Inserted `--` immediately before the pattern in both functions, matching the exact fix verified against real rg/grep in the issue report. While fixing this, found **three more call sites** with the identical bug, not cited in the original report: `_zero_match_probe()`'s own three separate rg invocations (a "why did this return zero matches" hint). Fixed all three identically. Verified the two `rg --files` (file-listing) call sites are NOT affected -- their pattern-shaped argument is the direct value of `-g`, unambiguous regardless of what it starts with. Left unchanged. ## Verification Verified end-to-end against real grep in this sandbox (rg isn't installed here): reproduced the exact reported error on unmodified code, confirmed it's gone after the fix. Added 5 regression tests. Verified as genuine regressions by stashing the entire fix and confirming all 5 fail against unmodified main. 91 pass / 4 skip (pre-existing) across the new test file plus four related search test files. One pre-existing, unrelated failure (multiline search requiring `rg` specifically, not installed in this sandbox) confirmed present identically on unmodified main.

signal.title: fix(tools): do not adopt a stale cwd after an interrupted command
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? A chat adopted the working directory of a different chat, and every later command in that chat ran there. The command wrapper prints the `__HERMES_CWD_*` marker after the command returns (`tools/environments/base.py:924`). A killed or timed-out command never prints it, so `env.cwd` still holds the directory of the last command that FINISHED. One local environment serves every session, because `_resolve_container_task_id` (`tools/terminal_tool.py:1384`) collapses cwd-only overrides to `"default"`. That leftover directory is therefore routinely another session's. Three call sites trusted a directory that the command never reported: - The post-command dual-write (`tools/terminal_tool.py:3315`) copied `env.cwd` into the interrupted session's durable record. - The cwd echo (`tools/terminal_tool.py:3422`) read the same value and told the model that it had moved. - The reaped-environment rescue (`tools/file_tools.py:1443`) copied a cached snapshot of the same shared value into the session record. Review found this sibling after the first version of this PR. This PR reports the observation instead of inferring it. The marker parse sets `result["cwd_observed"]`, and the two terminal-tool call sites read that flag. The file-tools rescue becomes fill-only: it writes the snapshot when the session has no record, and it never overwrites a record that the session wrote for itself. When a command reports no directory, the session keeps the directory that it already had. This approach is correct because the marker is the only evidence that a command finished somewhere. The parse already knows whether it found one, so the flag adds no new state and no new resolver. It also removes the last reads of the shared `env.cwd` on the session-record path, which the comment at `tools/terminal_tool.py:1180` asks for. ## Related Issue Fixes #85658 ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality) - [ ] 🔒 Security fix - [ ] 📝 Documentation update - [ ] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [ ] ♻️ Refactor (no behavior change) - [ ] 🎯 New skill (bundled or hub) ## Changes Made - `tools/environments/base.py` — `_extract_cwd_from_output` sets `result["cwd_observed"]` when the marker gives a directory for this command. The docstring states why an unobserved cwd belongs to no session. - `tools/environments/local.py` — the local override clears the flag when it rolls back a path that does not exist. The restored value is also unobserved. - `tools/terminal_tool.py` — the record write (line 3315) and the cwd echo (line 3422) both read the flag. - `tools/file_tools.py` — the rescue for a reaped environment (#26211) writes the cached snapshot only when the session has no record. The snapshot comes from the shared environment, so it is not attributable to the session. - `tests/tools/test_interrupted_command_cwd.py` — new. Eight tests against a real `LocalEnvironment`. Two of them drive `terminal_tool` itself through an interrupt, so the gates at the call sites have direct coverage. - `tests/tools/test_session_cwd_store.py` — two fakes simulate the marker parse. They moved `cwd` but did not report the observation, so they no longer modelled a completed command. They now return the flag. Two new tests pin the fill-only contract of the file-tools rescue. - `tests/tools/test_vercel_sandbox_environment.py` — two assertions compared the whole result dictionary against a literal. signal.title: [Bug]: An interrupted command adopts another session's working directory
signal.text: ### Bug Description A chat adopts the working directory of a different chat. This happens after a command in the first chat is interrupted or times out. Every later command in that chat then runs in the other chat's directory. The command wrapper prints the `__HERMES_CWD_*` marker after the command returns (`tools/environments/base.py:924`). A killed command never prints it, so `env.cwd` still holds the directory of the last command that FINISHED. One local environment serves every session. `_resolve_container_task_id` (`tools/terminal_tool.py:1384`) collapses cwd-only overrides to `"default"`. The leftover directory in `env.cwd` is therefore routinely another session's. The post-command dual-write (`tools/terminal_tool.py:3315`) copies `env.cwd` into the interrupted session's durable record. The cwd echo (`tools/terminal_tool.py:3422`) reads the same value and reports a move to the model. Both trust a directory that the command never reported. One session alone is sufficient to show this defect. A single session that interrupts a command also adopts a stale value. A second session only makes the wrong directory belong to another user of the app. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Open two desktop chats against one backend. 2. In chat A, run `cd /some/worktree && pwd`. Let it finish. 3. In chat B, run a long command such as `cd /other/dir && sleep 20`. 4. Interrupt the command in chat B, or let it time out. 5. In chat B, run `pwd`. This script reproduces the defect without the app: ```python import os, sys, tempfile sys.path.insert(0, ".") os.environ.pop("TERMINAL_ENV", None) import tools.terminal_tool as tt from tools.environments.local import LocalEnvironment repo = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="repo_") other = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="otherchat_") env = LocalEnvironment(cwd=os.path.expanduser("~"), timeout=30) env.init_session() def run(session_key, command, timeout=30): cwd = tt._resolve_command_cwd(workdir=None, default_cwd=env.cwd, session_key=session_key, env_type="local") r = env.execute(command, cwd=cwd, timeout=timeout) tt.record_session_cwd(session_key, getattr(env, "cwd", None)) return r run("mine", f"cd {repo} && pwd") run("other", f"cd {other} && pwd") run("mine", f"cd {repo} && sleep 20", timeout=2) # interrupted print("my record:", tt.get_session_cwd("mine")) print("expected :", repo) ``` ### Expected Behavior Chat B keeps its own directory. An interrupted command reports no directory, so the session keeps the directory that it already had. ### Actual Behavior Chat B adopts the directory of chat A. ``` shared env.cwd after other chat: /tmp/…/otherchat_4tfd78l7 my interrupted command: {'out': '[Command timed out after 2s]', 'exit': 124} my record became : /tmp/…/otherchat_4tfd78l7 <-- the other chat (repo was : /tmp/…/repo_217_imog ) ``` The live occurrence in the desktop app: chat `20260812_162559_09bcbf` worked in `.worktrees/ethie-desktop-bundles` and completed commands at t=1786644615.6 and t=1786644629.3. My chat ran `cd ~/src/hermes-agent && grep -rln …`, and the user interrupted it at t=1786644631.9. My record adopted the other chat's worktree, and `pwd` reported that worktree for the rest of the session. ### Affected Component Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.) ### Environment - OS: NixOS (Linux 7.1.0) - Surface: Desktop app, local backend - Commit: `ac9b9f54c` ### Notes The record store already carries a comment about this class of error (`tools/terminal_tool.py:1180`). It states that cwd state on the shared environment is a global that sessions timeshare. The write path still reads from that global. The docstring at `tools/terminal_tool.py:3303` claims that the record "never depends on the shared env surviving". That claim is true for a completed command and false for an interrupted one.

signal.title: [Bug]: Response truncated due to output length limit — still occurring after #7237 fix (re-opening closed issue)
signal.text: ### Bug Description The error "Response truncated due to output length limit" persists despite previous fixes in #7242 and #9525, which were merged in response to the now-closed issue #7237. The issue was closed by a maintainer last month with the explanation that it is "not a bug" but rather a context window limitation. However, extensive testing and user reports (see the 10+ comments since the closure) continue to reproduce the error across different models — including those with very large context windows (414k tokens, 131k tokens, and even Gemini 1.5 with 2M tokens). This suggests that while the **input context** might be sufficient, the **output token cap** or the **continuation logic** for long tool outputs/summaries is failing. This new issue is meant to re-surface the problem with specific reproduction data showing failures on fresh sessions with large-context models. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Launch `hermes chat` (CLI) or `hermes gateway start` (Telegram / Discord / Slack). 2. Trigger a tool call that returns a large, dense payload (e.g., >80KB). - *Example*: `mcp_mongodb_collection_schema` on a complex database collection. - *Example*: `read_file` on a large lockfile (e.g., `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `package-lock.json`). 3. Observe the agent stop mid-generation (often during a summary or a sub-agent's response) with: `:warning: Response truncated (finish_reason='length') - model hit max output tokens` `:warning: Truncated tool call response detected — refusing to execute incomplete tool arguments.` `Error: Response truncated due to output length limit` 4. This happens even on fresh sessions (low input context), ruling out simple history overflow. ### Expected Behavior Long responses should be split into chunks or the continuation logic should reliably retry until a complete response is assembled. The 3-retry mechanism introduced in #7242 / #9525 should prevent hard truncation in all API modes (chat_completions and anthropic_messages) by detecting `finish_reason='length'` and requesting the remainder. ### Actual Behavior The agent throws "Response truncated due to output length limit" and halts. The continuation/retry logic does not trigger effectively, or the truncated JSON/summary is rejected by the agent's core before it can be completed. Confirmed still occurring in: - qwen3.6-27b-fp8 (414k context) — @theogravity - GLM-51-NVFP4 — @Damikk19 - gpt-oss-20b (131k context) — @kevinctofel - aws-claude-opus-4-6 — @yangyang233333 - Gemini 1.5 Flash / Pro (2M context) — @poulpe-agent-repro - custom provider: gpt-5.5 — @arsitekberotok ### Affected Component Agent Core (conversation loop, tool output handling, continuation logic) ### Debug Report ```shell Report <https://paste.rs/JFt5G> agent.log <https://paste.rs/Anyts> gateway.log <https://paste.rs/N8CNm> ``` ### Operating System Ubuntu 24.04 ### Root Cause Analysis The current logic fails to differentiate between "Context Window Full" (Input) and "Max Output Tokens Hit" (Output). - Many providers have a hard limit on single completion length (e.g., 4096 or 8192 tokens). - When a tool returns a massive result (e.g., a 100KB schema), the model tries to process/summarize it and hits its output cap long before it exhausts its input context. - The continuation loop's progressive max_tokens boost (capped at 32k per #9525) might be insufficient or is not correctly detecting truncation when it happens inside a tool-call or sub-agent structure. ### Proposed Fix - **Intelligent Tool Output Management**: If a tool result exceeds a certain size (e.g., 50KB), save it to a temporary file and only inject a summary/snippet into the context to prevent the model from "choking" on the output generation. - **Unify Continuation Logic**: Ensure `anthropic_messages` and `chat_completions` paths are perfectly synced regarding truncation detection and retry. - **Configurable Output Caps**: Allow users to override the 32k boost cap or the default `max_tokens` for completions in `config.yaml`. - **Improved Logging**: Surface the actual token counts (Output used / Max output) when a truncation occurs to distinguish from Input context limits. ### Are you willing to submit a PR for this? - [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

signal.title: feat(status): surface memory pressure and suspected-OOM restarts to users (NS-656)
signal.text: ## Summary Hosted agents can be OOM-killed hourly while the dashboard looks perfectly healthy — every memory signal the gateway already produces (heartbeat mem samples, lifecycle-ledger unclean-exit verdicts, cache-pressure evictions) dies in server-side log files. The BlueAtlas incident (NS-608) ran for **three days** in an hourly OOM-restart loop with zero user-visible indication. This PR is the read-side fix: distill the *already-persisted* signals into a `memory` block on `/api/status` and render a dashboard banner. No new sampling, no gateway IPC — two small file reads. Linear: **NS-656** (context: NS-608 lifecycle ledger, NS-657 OOM-hardening gaps, OOF-77). ## What's in it ### `gateway/memory_status.py` (new) - Reads the 30s loop heartbeat (`state/gateway.heartbeat`, which already embeds `sample_memory()` — gateway RSS, system MemAvailable/MemTotal, swap) and the lifecycle sentinel. - Produces `{pressure: ok|elevated|critical|unknown, gateway_rss_mb, system_total_mb, system_available_mb, swap_used_mb, sampled_at, last_boot_unclean, last_boot_suspected_oom}`. - **Staleness honesty**: heartbeats older than 150s (or future-dated — clock skew / restored snapshots) keep their numbers but degrade `pressure` to `unknown`, so a dead gateway's final gasp can't render a live "critical" banner forever. - Critical thresholds (<64 MiB or <5% available) deliberately mirror the lifecycle ledger's OOM-suspicion heuristics: if a memory level would make a subsequent unclean death "suspected OOM", the user should already have been warned at that level while the process was alive. ### `gateway/lifecycle_ledger.py` - `record_startup()` now carries `prior_unclean_exit` / `prior_suspected_oom` onto the reclaimed sentinel. Previously the verdict survived only in append-only diag prose (`gateway-exit-diag.log`) — machine-unreadable. Flags are scoped to the life following the crash; the next sentinel rewrite ages them out. ### `/api/status` (`hermes_cli/web_server.py`) - Serves the block, profile-aware (`?profile=` passes the resolved home through), executor-offloaded, and fail-safe: a crashing collector degrades to `{"pressure": "unknown"}` instead of 500ing the status endpoint. - **Deliberately NOT folded into `components`/`overall`**: memory pressure is advisory (toast/notice material), not a liveness verdict — flipping `overall` to `degraded` on it would page NAS's availability sweep for a condition the cache-eviction valve is already handling. - Public-safety: this endpoint is unauthenticated (`PUBLIC_API_PATHS`) — which is exactly why NAS can consume it. The block carries only coarse MB numbers, enums, and booleans: same disclosure class as the existing `nous_session_valid` field, which was added for the same NAS-sweep audience. ### Dashboard (`web/`) - New `MemoryPressureBanner` in the app shell (next to `ProfileScopeBanner`), driven by the existing 10s sidebar status poll — no new requests. - Worst-first trigger precedence: `critical` > suspected-OOM restart > `elevated`. Copy: *"Your agent restarted after running out of memory"* / *"Your agent is almost out of memory and may restart"*. - Per-trigger session-scoped dismissal; escalation (elevated → critical) re-opens past a dismissal. `pressure: "unknown"` renders nothing — absence of evidence is not evidence of health, but it's not banner material either. - i18n keys optional with English fallbacks (matches the `managingProfileBanner` convention). ## What's NOT in it - NAS-side ingestion (persisting the block from the availability sweep, agent-card notice, memory-tier upsell) ships separately on nous-account-service. - Prevention work (memory-aware kanban worker cap, reclaim-storm breaker, dashboard RSS bounds) is tracked in NS-657. ## Testing - `tests/gateway/test_memory_status.py`: classification bands, absolute-floor-without-total, `True`-is-not-an-int guard, staleness, future-dated heartbeats, corrupt files never raise, missing mem block (non-Linux). - `tests/gateway/test_lifecycle_ledger.py`: sentinel carry-forward on unclean+OOM boot; clean boot leaves no flags. - `tests/hermes_cli/test_web_server.py::TestStatusMemoryBlock`: block always present; collector crash degrades instead of 500. - `web/src/components/MemoryPressureBanner.test.tsx`: 7 tests covering trigger selection, precedence, dismissal, escalation re-open. - Full runs: 176 passed / 2 skipped (targeted gateway+web_server suites), ruff clean, `tsc` clean, eslint clean, vitest 7/7.

signal.title: feat(relay): live-card ops — native draft streaming + task cards over the relay (gateway half)
signal.text: ## Summary Gateway half of bringing #85476's Slack live cards (native `chat.startStream` reply streaming + plan/task-card tool progress) to **relayed** Slack, where the connector is the platform adapter. Connector half follows in the gateway-gateway repo; internal tracking NS-658. ## Design Three additive ops within relay contract v1, emitted only when the connector's negotiated descriptor advertises them: ``` {op: "draft", chat_id, draft_id, content, final, metadata} {op: "task_card", chat_id, card_id, chunks, metadata} {op: "task_card_stop", chat_id, card_id, metadata} ``` The gateway side is deliberately dumb — no Slack API knowledge, no new config keys. Slack mechanics (the three stream calls, per-workspace feature-gate cache, send+edit fallback) live connector-side, matching the relay model's ownership split. **The semantic bridge (the interesting part):** the base `send_draft` contract is Telegram-shaped — the draft clears and the final answer arrives as a separate `send()`. Slack native streaming inverts that: the stream IS the message, sealed once. The relay adapter tracks the open draft per chat and converts the turn-final `send()` into `draft(final=true)`, so the connector seals the stream instead of posting a duplicate; the stream ts returns as the message identity. A failed draft frame disarms the interception, so the stream consumer's existing edit-based fallback path delivers a real send untouched. **Task cards** ride #85476's adapter-agnostic TurnRunner seam (`hasattr` on `send_native_task_card_progress`); `supports_native_task_cards()` is the descriptor probe, and the raw normalized task dicts cross the wire — 256-char chunk-field limits are enforced connector-side where the API lives. ## Behavior change (deliberate, fenced) Relay `supports_draft_streaming()` now requires the descriptor flag **and** the `draft` op. Flag-only was a latent lie: `send_draft` inherited `NotImplementedError`, so a connector setting the flag without an op would have crashed the stream consumer's draft path at runtime. `supported_ops` remains fail-open for legacy (pre-contract) ops; `draft`/`task_card` did not exist pre-contract and must not fail open. Every currently-deployed connector advertises `supports_draft_streaming: false`, so no deployed behavior changes. ## Validation | Check | Result | |---|---| | New suite `tests/gateway/relay/test_relay_live_cards.py` | 12 passed | | Full relay suite | 189 passed | | Gates: relay + stream-consumer draft + Slack suites (canonical runner) | **365 passed, 0 failed** | | Mutation check (seal interception disabled) | exactly the 2 seal tests fail; restore → green | Cross-repo live E2E harness pair (`connector_slack_stream_harness.mjs` + driver) lands with the connector half.

signal.title: fix(desktop): preserve multi-pane plugins when closing panes
signal.text: ## What & why Closing a pane contributed by a plugin previously disabled the **entire plugin**, unloading every one of its contributions. For a plugin that owns several independent panes — e.g. Bot Mode's Cronjobs pane alongside its Bots roster and composer middleware — closing one pane silently killed the rest. Now, closing a pane from a multi-pane plugin **dismisses only that pane**: the plugin stays enabled and its other panes, commands, and middleware keep working. **Reset layout** restores dismissed contributed panes. A single-pane plugin keeps the existing symmetric behavior (Close disables the plugin, with **Settings → Plugins** as the discoverable recovery path). ## How to test 1. Install a multi-pane plugin (e.g. Hermes-Bot-Mode) and open two of its panes. 2. Close one pane (e.g. Cronjobs) — it disappears; the plugin's other pane (Bots roster) stays functional. 3. Confirm the plugin is still enabled in **Settings → Plugins**. 4. Reset layout — the dismissed pane returns. 5. Single-pane plugin: closing its only pane still disables the plugin. Regression coverage: `apps/desktop/src/components/pane-shell/tree/plugin-pane-close.test.ts` (multi-pane dismiss, dismissal surviving pane adoption, single-pane disable). ## Platforms tested - Linux desktop UI test suite: 3,829 tests passed (426 files), ESLint clean. ## Related No related issue — reported directly from the Hermes-Bot-Mode plugin user experience.

signal.title: fix(voice): global playback arbitration — one sound at a time across sessions
signal.text: ## Summary Fix the TTS **audio-stacking (叠音)** bug: concurrent playback requests from different sessions/windows/processes could run **multiple `afplay` streams at once**, because `play_audio_file()` stored the current player in a global reference but a new request never interrupted the previous one — it just overwrote the reference. **One sound at a time, everywhere.** Latest request wins (barge-in), matching the existing `stop_playback()` semantics. ## Problem - Hermes Desktop renders multiple sessions against one backend `serve` process; a separate `gateway` process may run alongside. - `play_audio_file()` spawns a system player (`afplay` on macOS) and records it in the module-global `_active_playback` under `_playback_lock`. - A second concurrent request **overwrote** the reference instead of interrupting the first player → both players ran → audio layering. - The renderer's sequence guard (`voice-playback.ts`) ran only **after** backend playback had already started → couldn't prevent the overlap. **Repro:** two sessions hit read-aloud within ~100ms → two `afplay` processes coexist → 叠音. ## Fix (3 parts) 1. **In-process arbitration** — before spawning any player, atomically (under `_playback_lock`) terminate the previous `_active_playback`, bounded-wait (0.5s) for it to exit, then spawn + record the new one. `proc.wait()` stays outside the lock so `stop_playback()` can still interrupt mid-play. 2. **Cross-process arbitration** — a shared pidfile `HERMES_HOME/tts/.audio-playback.pid` records the current player. Before spawning, `_interrupt_other_process_playback()` reads it, verifies the PID still names a system audio player (`ps -p <pid> -o comm=` — guards against **PID reuse killing an unrelated process**), terminates it, and waits for exit. The new player records its own PID; ownership-checked `_clear_playback_pid()` removes it on completion or stop. 3. **No fall-through after interrupt** — a superseded (`was_current=False`) or signal-killed (`rc < 0`) player returns `False` instead of falling through to the next player in the list (`afplay → ffplay → aplay`). Re-spawning would re-layer the very stream we were interrupted on and defeat the arbitration. ## Behavior contract - One sound at a time **per process** and **across processes** sharing `HERMES_HOME`. - Latest request wins (barge-in); the interrupted call reports `False`. - `stop_playback()` (`/api/audio/stop`) still works and clears both the in-process slot and the pidfile. - Normal completion reports `True`; the pidfile is removed only by its owner. - No credential change — existing `hermes_subprocess_env(inherit_credentials=False)` scrub unchanged; players never inherit gateway tokens/API keys. - Best-effort: `ps`/file failures are swallowed — playback never blocks on arbitration. ## Why a pidfile and not flock / a daemon? | Option | Verdict | |--------|---------| | **PID file + verified-comm kill** | ~60 LOC, no new infra, PID-reuse guard, works across unrelated processes | | `flock` (blocking) | Queue semantics — a hung player blocks everyone; can't *interrupt* | | Unified audio daemon | Cleanest but a new long-running service — disproportionate for playback | See `docs/security/DECISION-RECORD-tts-playback-arbitration.md`. ## Security design The only privileged primitive (cross-process `SIGTERM`) is gated behind a verified-comm allowlist (`afplay`/`ffplay`/`aplay`); pidfile content is int-parse guarded (`pid <= 0` short-circuits); kill+spawn is atomic under the non-reentrant lock (no nested `stop_playback()` call → no deadlock); all player spawns keep the pre-existing credential scrub. Full audit: `docs/security/SECURITY-AUDIT-tts-playback-arbitration.md` Baseline: `docs/security/SECURITY-BASELINE-tts-playback-arbitration.md` ## Self-test (macOS, M5 Max) - **New tests** — `TestPlaybackArbitration` (3) + `TestCrossProcessArbitration` (4): **7/7 pass**. - **Full suite** — 63 passed; 3 pre-existing environment-only failures (sounddevice beep test + 2 WSL-only tests); **zero regression** vs baseline (57 passed / 3 failed before the change). - **Real concurrent plays** (2 threads, 4s+2s WAVs) — `afplay` peak = 1; first call interrupted, second completes. - **Real cross-process plays** (2 independent Python processes) — first process's player interrupted by the second; `afplay` peak = 1; no residue; pidfile cleaned. ## Who should enable No opt-in needed — this is a bug fix for everyone who uses TTS playback (desktop read-aloud, voice-conversation mode, CLI/TUI voice, gateway audio). The pidfile path is derived from `HERMES_HOME`; nothing to configure. ## Platform compatibility - **macOS** — primary target (`afplay` path), fully tested. - **Linux / WSL** — same code path (`ffplay`/`aplay` + PowerShell fallback); the arbitration guards are platform-neutral; WSL-specific tests unaffected. - **Windows** — system-player list is empty there; `play_audio_file` already falls through; arbitration adds no new platform calls (`ps` is only invoked on POSIX; on Windows the comm check fails closed → no cross-process kill). ## Quick-start Nothing to do — restart the backend and the fix is live. To observe it: ```bash # Terminal 1 — long playback afplay -t 5 /path/to/a.wav & # or any Hermes read-aloud # Terminal 2 — new playback interrupts it afplay /path/to/b.wav # Hermes: a second session's read-aloud ``` Only the newest sound is heard; the old one stops within ~50ms. ## Troubleshooting | Symptom | Cause | Fix | |---------|-------|-----| | Two sounds still overlap | Backend not restarted after upgrade | Restart `serve`/desktop; both processes must run the new code | | No sound at all | `afplay` missing / no output device | Pre-existing behavior unchanged; check `which afplay` | | Stale `tts/.audio-playback.pid` | Process crashed mid-play | Harmless — next play verifies the PID via `ps`, fails closed, overwrites | | Cross-process kill not happening | `ps` unavailable (non-POSIX) | Fails closed by design (no kill); in-process arbitration still applies |

signal.title: Inspired by Copilot CLI: plugin auto-update at session start + update --all
signal.text: ## Summary Git-installed plugins can now keep themselves current: `hermes plugins update --all` sweeps every git-installed plugin in one command, and `hermes plugins autoupdate <name> on` opts a plugin into a background pull at session start (throttled to once per 24h) — updated code takes effect the next session, so the live session's plugin registry and prompt cache are never touched. Inspired by GitHub Copilot CLI v1.0.79 ([changelog](https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/blob/main/changelog.md)): *"Set `autoUpdate: true` on an extraKnownMarketplaces entry in your user settings to auto-update its plugins at session start."* ## Their mechanism → our adaptation Copilot CLI auto-updates marketplace plugins at session start via a per-marketplace settings flag. Hermes plugins are individual git checkouts (not marketplace buckets), so the opt-in is **per plugin**, stored in the existing install-metadata sidecar (`~/.hermes/plugins/.install-metadata.json`). The sweep rides the existing background plugin-discovery thread and runs strictly **after** discovery completes, so it can never race the imports of the session that triggered it — a deliberate divergence from Copilot's update-then-load ordering, forced by our prompt-caching invariant (a mid-session plugin reload would rebuild the system prompt). ## Changes - `hermes_cli/plugins_cmd.py`: `_iter_updatable_plugins()`, `_update_one_plugin_dir()` (shared single-plugin pull: pinned-skip, revision recording, stale-bytecode clear), `_update_all_plugins()` sweep, `cmd_autoupdate()` (on/off/show; rejects pinned + non-git plugins), `run_startup_auto_update_sweep()` (24h stamp-file throttle, never raises), dispatch wiring. - `hermes_cli/plugins.py`: background discovery thread calls the sweep after `discover_and_load()` + toolset-key persistence. - `hermes_cli/subcommands/plugins.py`: `update` gains optional name + `--all`; new `autoupdate` subparser. - `website/docs/user-guide/features/plugins.md`: command table + auto-update semantics (next-session effect, pinned exclusion, fail-closed capabilities). - `tests/hermes_cli/test_plugins_autoupdate.py`: 20 tests, real-git E2E for pull/revision/bytecode/throttle paths. ## Safety properties - Pinned (`--ref`) plugins are never auto-updated and can't be opted in. - Non-interactive updates leave newly declared capabilities **ungranted** (fail closed) — same contract as the existing dashboard update path; interactive `hermes plugins update <name>` still runs the re-consent prompt. - Local edits survive via the existing autostash pull (`_git_pull_plugin_dir`). - Sweep is throttled by a stamp file in `~/.hermes/cache/` and logs failures instead of raising into the discovery thread. ## Validation | | Result | |---|---| | New tests (`test_plugins_autoupdate.py`) | 20/20 pass | | Existing plugin tests (`test_plugins_cmd.py`, `test_plugin_install_ref.py`) | 68/68 pass | | E2E (temp HERMES_HOME, real argparse → `hermes plugins autoupdate/update --all`, real git origins) | enable → flag persisted → `update --all` pulls → startup sweep pulls flagged plugin only → second sweep throttled | ## Infographic ![Plugin Auto-Update infographic](https://files.catbox.moe/1aqjbs.png)

signal.title: Add gateway.non_conversational guard for cron-only profiles
signal.text: Hermes supports cron-only gateway processes: a gateway with zero messaging platforms can still tick cron. For security-sensitive scheduled runners, operators need a first-class config option that makes a profile explicitly non-conversational and fails gateway startup if any messaging platform is enabled. Proposed shape: - config: `gateway.non_conversational: true` - startup behavior: before platform adapter creation, if any `platforms.*.enabled=true`, write `startup_failed` runtime status and exit with fatal config code - multiplex behavior: if the default gateway serves a secondary profile with `gateway.non_conversational=true` and any enabled platform, abort multiplexer startup with a config error - use case: split request intake from scheduled execution so conversational agents can record desired alerts while a separate cron-only profile runs them without any chat surface This avoids relying on documentation or systemd `ExecStartPre` alone, both of which are bypassable via direct `hermes --profile <name> gateway run`.

signal.title: [Bug]: search_files fails on any pattern starting with "-" — missing "--" separator before the pattern (affects both the rg and grep paths)
signal.text: Summary search_files builds its shell command without the -- end-of-options separator before the pattern argument. Any search pattern that begins with - is therefore parsed as a flag by the underlying binary, and the search fails. This is not a quoting problem — _escape_shell_arg correctly wraps the pattern in single quotes, so the shell passes it as one argument. The issue is that rg/grep themselves treat a leading - as an option. The failure is silent from the agent's point of view: the tool returns total_count: 0 with an error string, and in an unattended context (cron job) the run still reports ok, so the model produces an incomplete answer that looks complete. Environment Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (2026.8.3) Install dir: /opt/hermes, Python 3.13.5 Docker (nousresearch/hermes-agent), Debian-based image ripgrep 14.1.1 at /usr/bin/rg (present and working) Reproduction Ask the agent to search for a Markdown task checkbox, which is an extremely common pattern in note vaults: search_files(pattern="- [ ]", path=".", target="content") Result: {"total_count": 0, "error": "Search failed: rg: unrecognized flag - "} Reproduced directly with the exact command shape the tool builds: $ rg --line-number --no-heading --with-filename '- [ ]' . rg: unrecognized flag - $ rg --line-number --no-heading --with-filename -- '- [ ]' . ./notes/Project.md:42:- [ ] pending task The grep fallback has the identical defect: $ grep -rnHE --exclude-dir='.*' '- [ ]' . grep: invalid option -- ' ' $ grep -rnHE --exclude-dir='.*' -- '- [ ]' . ./notes/Project.md:42:- [ ] pending task Root cause tools/file_operations.py, two places, both missing --: 1. _search_with_rg (defined at line 2543), lines 2572-2573: # Add pattern and path cmd_parts.append(self._escape_shell_arg(pattern)) cmd_parts.append(self._escape_shell_arg(path)) 2. _search_with_grep (defined at line 2684), lines 2708-2709: identical two lines. Suggested fix Insert the separator immediately before the pattern in both functions: # Add pattern and path. `--` stops option parsing so a pattern that # starts with "-" (e.g. the Markdown checkbox "- [ ]") is not read as a flag. cmd_parts.append("--") cmd_parts.append(self._escape_shell_arg(pattern)) cmd_parts.append(self._escape_shell_arg(path)) Both rg and GNU grep accept -- in that position, verified above. Impact Any pattern beginning with - is unsearchable. The most common real-world case is the Markdown task checkbox - [ ], plus list items, diff-style lines (-foo), and CLI flags being grepped for in code or logs. The failure mode matters as much as the failure. In a scheduled/cron context there is no user present to notice the tool error, the job still completes with status ok, and the delivered report is quietly missing whatever that search would have found. Workaround Escape the leading character so the pattern no longer starts with - — e.g. search \[ \] instead of - [ ]. This has to be enforced in the prompt, which is fragile: the model will "helpfully" revert to the natural pattern unless it is told why not to.

signal.title: fix(desktop): keep non-ASCII MEDIA filenames intact in mediaName()
signal.text: Fixes #84588, fixes #85257. > Built on top of #68788 by @mhtsai888 (applied via `git am`, authorship preserved) — this adds the filesystem-path bypass and closes the literal-`%` regression. See "Relation to existing PRs" below. ## Problem In the Desktop app, a `MEDIA:` attachment whose path contains non-ASCII characters renders a percent-encoded label — e.g. `File: %E6%9C%AA%E5%85%B3%E8%81%94...xlsx` instead of `File: 未关联门店...xlsx`. Root cause in `mediaName()` (`apps/desktop/src/lib/media.ts`): every path is routed through `new URL()`. A Windows drive letter (`D:`) parses as a URL **scheme** under WHATWG rules, so: 1. The `catch` string-split branch is dead code for exactly the paths Desktop produces most (`MEDIA:` artifact deliveries); 2. The URL parser percent-encodes non-ASCII characters in `pathname`; 3. For non-special schemes, backslashes are not path separators, so `split('/')` returns the entire percent-encoded remainder as a single segment. Repro (Windows, local mode): have the agent emit ``` MEDIA:D:\dir\码上编码对照统计\报告.xlsx ``` → the chat label renders `File: \dir\%E7%A0%81%E4%B8%8A...%E6%8A%A5%E5%91%8A.xlsx`. ## Fix Two commits: 1. **From #68788 (@mhtsai888)** — dual-separator split (`split(/[\\/]/)`) + defensive `decodeURIComponent` wrapper. 2. **Added in this PR** — filesystem paths (`D:\…`/`D:/…`, `\\unc\…`, `~/…`, `/…`) bypass `new URL()` entirely, and decoding applies **only to URL-parser output**, so genuine on-disk filenames containing literal `%` sequences (`a%20b.txt`) are no longer corrupted into `a b.txt`. ## Relation to existing PRs - **#84631** — handles drive letters but never decodes the URL branch (https/file URLs with CJK names stay encoded), has no tests, and bundles an unrelated `agent/model_metadata.py` pricing change. - **#84635** — close to correct, but `decodeURIComponent` is unguarded: a URL like `https://example.com/100%.txt` throws `URIError` while rendering the label. No `file://` coverage. - **#68788** (base of this PR) — has the guarded decode and dual-separator split, but applies decode uniformly, so real on-disk names with literal `%` (`D:\dir\a%20b.txt`) get wrongly decoded to `a b.txt`; it also relies on opaque-path quirks of non-special URL schemes to survive drive letters rather than bypassing URL parsing for filesystem paths. Happy to rebase/close if the maintainers prefer to land one of the others first. ## Tests 13 `mediaName` cases added/covered in `media.remote.test.ts`: Windows backslash & forward-slash CJK paths, paths with spaces, UNC, `~`, POSIX absolute, `file://` percent-encoded CJK, malformed `%` escapes, https URL decode, literal-`%` preservation (absolute + relative), plain-URL / relative-path / no-path-segment regressions. Verified on Windows 10: - `vitest run src/lib/media.remote.test.ts src/lib/chat-messages.test.ts` — **85/85 ✅** - `vitest run src/lib` — **685/685 ✅** (72 files) - `npm run typecheck` — **✅** (all three tsconfigs)

signal.text: fix(agent): flatten list-typed delta.content/reasoning in auxiliary stream accumulator and reasoning path Some OpenAI-compatible providers (e.g. GLM via custom proxies likes NewAPI) return delta.content or delta.reasoning_content as a list of content-part dicts rather than a plain string. Two sites remained unprotected: 1. `_ChatStreamAccumulator.feed()` in `agent/auxiliary_client.py` — the auxiliary client's stream aggregator passed raw `delta.content` into `content_parts` (joined with `"".join` later → `TypeError`) and only accepted str-typed `reasoning_piece` (list reasoning was silently dropped). Apply `flatten_message_text()` to both paths. 2. The `reasoning_text` path in `interruptible_streaming_api_call()` in `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py` — `delta.reasoning_content` as a list would crash on `.strip()` in `_fire_reasoning_delta`. Apply `flatten_message_text()` before the reasoning accumulator and callback. The `delta.content` path in `interruptible_streaming_api_call()` is already covered by PR #63755 and is intentionally NOT duplicated here. Complements #63755 (which handles `delta.content` in the main streaming loop). Fixes #63734 for the auxiliary and reasoning paths. ## What does this PR do? Fixes two streaming-delta sites where list-typed `delta.content` or `delta.reasoning_content` from OpenAI-compatible providers (e.g. GLM via NewAPI proxies) would crash or silently drop data. These sites are **not** covered by the open PR #63755, which handles `delta.content` in the main streaming loop of `interruptible_streaming_api_call()`. **Site 1 — `_ChatStreamAccumulator.feed()`** (`agent/auxiliary_client.py`): the auxiliary client's stream aggregator passed raw `delta.content` into `content_parts`, which later gets `"".join()`-ed — a list value causes `TypeError`. signal.title: hermes skills update blocked when HERMES_HOME is a Windows junction (physical vs junction path mismatch)
signal.text: ## Summary `hermes skills update` fails for every skill when `HERMES_HOME` lives on a **Windows directory junction** (e.g. `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\hermes` → `D:\hermes`). All updates are blocked by the install-path validation with: ``` Installation blocked: 'D:\hermes\skills\<skill>' is not in the subpath of 'C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\hermes\skills' OR one path is relative and the other is absolute. ``` ## Environment - OS: Windows - Hermes: v0.20.0 (2026.8.3) - Python: 3.11.15 - `HERMES_HOME=C:\Users\xianff\AppData\Local\hermes` is a **junction** → `D:\hermes` ## Root cause When `HERMES_HOME` is a Windows junction, `Path.resolve()` in `_resolve_lock_install_path()` (tools/skills_hub.py) returns the **physical** path (`D:\hermes\skills\<skill>`), but the subsequent `is_relative_to()` / `relative_to()` comparison uses the **junction-form** skills dir (`C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\hermes\skills`). The drive-letter mismatch makes the check fail, so every `hermes skills update` is blocked — even though the skill is already installed and the target is legitimately inside the skills directory. This blocks the **update** path (`hermes skills update`). Related symptom also affects `hermes skills install` for new skills. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Set up `HERMES_HOME` under a Windows directory junction pointing to a physical dir on another drive (e.g. `mklink /J C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\hermes D:\hermes`). 2. Run `hermes skills check` → shows N skills `update_available`. 3. Run `hermes skills update`. 4. Every skill reports `Installation blocked: '<physical path>' is not in the subpath of '<junction path>'`. ## Expected behavior `hermes skills update` should update skills whose directory resolves (via junction/symlink) to a location inside the skills root — the junction is a legitimate filesystem layout, not a path escape. ## Related - PR #76885 "fix(skills): resolve install path against resolved skills dir (Windows junction)" — author's root-cause analysis matches this exactly, but it is **not yet merged** (blocked on requested E2E regression test). - #35674 — symlinked skills trigger false "outside trusted skills directory" warning (same junction/symlink resolution root cause). - #63369 — `hermes skills install` hit the same `subpath of` ValueError on Windows + git-bash.

signal.title: fix(agent): explain per-turn search caps without false retry claims
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? When distinct web searches reach the per-turn cap, Hermes currently describes them as repeated non-progressing attempts. That diagnosis is inaccurate and can send users toward the wrong recovery action even though the searches were all different. This change formats count-cap halt responses according to their decision codes. Web-search and subagent caps now report the per-turn limit they actually enforce, while repetition guardrails keep their existing retry-oriented explanation. ### Symptom After 50 distinct `web_search` calls in one turn, the next call is blocked with `loop_web_search_cap`, but the final response says the agent made 50 repeated non-progressing attempts. ### Impact Users who legitimately exhaust the search budget receive a false explanation of why execution stopped. The message incorrectly implies duplicated work instead of identifying the per-turn limit and advising the user to continue from collected results or change strategy. ### Bug Cause **Trigger:** `run_agent.py` / `AIAgent._toolguard_controlled_halt_response()` formats a controlled halt after the guardrail controller returns a count-cap decision. **Causal chain:** 1. Distinct `web_search` calls increment the unconditional per-turn search counter. 2. The next call returns `loop_web_search_cap` after the configured count is reached. 3. A generic halt formatter describes every decision as repeated non-progressing attempts, producing a false user-facing diagnosis. **Why it is wrong:** Count caps measure total calls in a turn, not repeated arguments or lack of progress, so repetition wording does not describe the decision that stopped execution. **Working sibling / contrast:** Exact-failure and idempotent no-progress guardrails do track repeated behavior, so their retry-oriented message remains unchanged. The sibling `loop_subagent_cap` count decision now receives the same code-aware treatment to prevent the same false diagnosis there. **Ruled out:** The controller's counters and decision metadata are already correct. Controller-driven tests confirm that distinct inputs are allowed until the configured cap and then produce the expected count-cap code. ### Fix Add decision-code-specific controlled halt messages for web-search and subagent per-turn caps, and cover both paths with controller-driven regression tests using distinct inputs. ## Related Issue Closes #85746 ## Type of Change - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) ## Changes Made - `run_agent.py` - report web-search and subagent count caps as per-turn limits. - `tests/run_agent/test_tool_call_guardrail_runtime.py` - verify code-aware halt messages after distinct searches and subagent tasks. ## How to Test 1. Configure small web-search and subagent loop caps. 2. Submit distinct inputs until each cap is reached. 3. Confirm the controlled halt names the applicable per-turn limit and does not call the inputs repeated non-progressing attempts. 4. Run the targeted guardrail tests: ```bash scripts/run_tests.sh tests/agent/test_tool_guardrail_runtime.py tests/run_agent/test_tool_call_guardrail_runtime.py -k 'web_search_cap or subagent_cap' ``` Result: 3 passed. ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) (`fix(scope):`, `feat(scope):`, etc.) - [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate - [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix/feature (no unrelated commits) - [x] I've run the repo test entry on the relevant guardrail tests and all tests pass - [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes, strongly encouraged for features) - [x] I've tested on my platform: Windows 11 ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] I've updated relevant documentation (README, `docs/`, docstrings) - N/A; no user-facing documentation contract changed - [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` if I added/changed config keys - N/A; no configuration changed - [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` if I changed architecture or workflows - N/A; no architecture or workflow changed - [x] I've considered cross-platform impact (Windows, macOS) per the [compatibility guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#cross-platform-compatibility) - pure response formatting is platform-independent - [x] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas if I changed tool behavior - N/A; tool execution and schemas are unchanged

signal.title: Desktop per-profile remote overrides silently relabel sessions from multi-profile backends
signal.text: ## Bug description Hermes Desktop silently misattributes sessions when multiple Desktop profiles use per-profile remote overrides that point to the same multi-profile Hermes backend. Concrete setup: - One remote Hermes host/backend contains `default`, `wife`, and `dad` profiles. - Desktop → Settings → Gateway configures the `wife` scope and `dad` scope with the same remote backend URL, intending each Desktop profile to use its matching remote profile. - Switching between `wife` and `dad` does not reliably distinguish their sessions. Rows from the remote backend's launch/current profile can appear under whichever local Desktop profile selected the connection. This is a real user workflow, not hypothetical: the user shares one Hermes host with family profiles and needs Desktop session history to preserve the remote profile boundary. ## Reproduction 1. Run one remote `hermes serve` backend on a host with at least two named profiles, e.g. `wife` and `dad`. 2. In Hermes Desktop, open Settings → Gateway. 3. Under **Applies to**, configure `wife` as Remote and point it at that backend URL. 4. Configure `dad` the same way, pointing at the same backend URL. 5. Create or observe distinct sessions in the remote `wife` and `dad` profile databases. 6. Switch between the two Desktop profiles and inspect the session list. ### Actual The session list does not preserve the remote owning profile. It can show the backend launch-profile sessions under both Desktop scopes, relabeled as `wife` or `dad`. ### Expected Desktop must either: 1. route each request to the explicit matching remote profile and preserve authoritative profile identity returned by the backend; or 2. detect that a per-profile override is not a profile-scoped endpoint and block/warn instead of silently relabeling sessions. The UI must never claim that a session belongs to `wife` or `dad` unless the backend request was actually scoped to that profile. ## Root cause on current `main` The per-profile remote override path assumes that each URL already serves exactly one profile: - `apps/desktop/electron/connection-config.ts` documents that per-profile remote overrides are already profile-scoped and therefore omits the profile query. - `apps/desktop/electron/main.ts::remoteSessionList` deletes `profile` from the query, calls the remote backend's ordinary `/api/sessions`, then forcibly assigns every returned row to the local Desktop profile: ```ts qs.delete('profile') const data = await fetchJsonForProfile(profile, `/api/sessions?${qs}`) for (const s of rowsOf(data)) { s.profile = profile s.is_default_profile = false } ``` Against a multi-profile backend, `/api/sessions` therefore reads the backend process's launch/current profile, and Desktop overwrites that authoritative identity with the local connection-scope name. This is distinct from, but interacts with, #62503 / #62509: - #62509 fixes backend `session.*` RPC methods that ignore `params.profile`. - #64266 proposes explicit `session_profiles` capability negotiation and authoritative profile echoes. - This issue is the Desktop REST/session-list path and connection semantics: a per-profile override currently strips profile scope and manufactures profile labels. ## Suggested direction Use backend capability/identity rather than assuming URL shape: - If the remote advertises profile-aware routing, keep/pass the requested profile (`?profile=<name>` / `params.profile`) and preserve the backend-returned profile. - If the endpoint is explicitly profile-scoped, verify its effective profile before using it and tag rows only from that verified identity. - Never unconditionally overwrite `s.profile` merely because that local connection entry was selected. - Add a regression with one remote URL, two Desktop profile scopes, and distinct session rows in two remote profile databases. - Consider a Settings warning when two per-profile overrides share one URL but the backend cannot prove profile-aware routing. ## Environment note `HERMES_DESKTOP_REMOTE_URL` was verified unset in the shell, macOS `launchctl`, and all running Hermes Desktop processes. The behavior comes from saved per-profile connection overrides, not the environment override.

signal.title: feat(browser): support Camofox cookie import (#6109)
signal.text: Closes #6109. ## Summary Adds a new `browser_import_cookies` tool that imports Netscape-format `cookies.txt` files into a live Camofox session, so agents can authenticate to sites like LinkedIn or Amazon without interactive login every run. The upstream [camofox-browser](https://github.com/jo-inc/camofox-browser) already exposes `POST /sessions/:userId/cookies` with a Bearer-token auth gate; this PR wires that endpoint up on the Hermes side. ## What changed - **`tools/browser_camofox.py`** — new `_netscape_parse`, `_resolve_cookies_dir`, `_read_cookie_file`, and `camofox_import_cookies` functions. Parser mirrors upstream `lib/cookies.js` (BOM, `#HttpOnly_` prefix, CRLF, embedded-tab values). - **`tools/browser_tool.py`** — new `browser_import_cookies` delegate + schema entry + registry registration with a camofox-only `check_fn` so Browserbase / Firecrawl / agent-browser users don't see an unusable tool. - **`hermes_cli/config.py`** — two new env vars: `CAMOFOX_API_KEY` (secret) and `CAMOFOX_COOKIES_DIR`. - **`hermes_cli/tools_config.py`** — optional fields in the Camofox provider's setup flow. - **`tests/conftest.py`** — whitelist `CAMOFOX_COOKIES_DIR` in the hermetic-env fixture. - **Docs** — `website/docs/user-guide/features/browser.md` (new "Cookie import" section) and `website/docs/reference/environment-variables.md` (two rows). ## Safety rails - Paths are resolved strictly inside `CAMOFOX_COOKIES_DIR` — traversal (`../secret`) and absolute paths are rejected (`ValueError`). - 5 MB file cap and 500-cookie cap enforced **client-side** before the server request. - Cookie body sanitized to Playwright allowlist (`name`, `value`, `domain`, `path`, `expires`, `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite`). - `CAMOFOX_API_KEY` registered with `password: True` so it gets redacted by downstream loaders. - Cookie values never logged — only counts + userId land in `hermes.log`. - Tool hidden from the schema unless `CAMOFOX_URL` is set (no cross-backend leakage). ## Test plan TDD throughout — 26 new tests, all green: - [x] `TestNetscapeParser` (7) — basic line, `#HttpOnly_`, comments, BOM, tab-embedded value, malformed-line skip, CRLF - [x] `TestReadCookieFile` (7) — in-dir read, `../` blocked, absolute-path blocked, 5MB cap, domain-suffix filter, missing file, default dir - [x] `TestCamofoxImportCookies` (8) — missing API key, Bearer header/body shape, field allowlist, 403/400 surfacing, 500-cookie cap, domain_suffix forwarding, empty-file error - [x] `TestBrowserImportCookiesRouting` (4) — delegation, non-camofox error, `check_fn` gating on/off - [x] `pytest tests/tools/test_browser_camofox.py tests/hermes_cli/test_config.py tests/hermes_cli/test_tools_config.py` → 128/128 pass Manual verification (run locally once camofox server is up): - [x] `openssl rand -hex 32` → set `CAMOFOX_API_KEY` on both server & Hermes - [x] Drop a real `cookies.txt` under `~/.camofox/cookies/` - [x] Ask the agent: "import my linkedin cookies and open feed" → expect authenticated session - [x] Unset `CAMOFOX_URL` → confirm tool disappears from schema ## References - Upstream spec: [jo-inc/camofox-browser README § Cookie Import](https://github.com/jo-inc/camofox-browser#cookie-import) - Upstream handler: `server.js:175-247` - Upstream parser mirrored in `tools/browser_camofox.py::_netscape_parse`

signal.title: feat(deepseek): support Responses API native web search
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Adds first-class, model-aware DeepSeek Responses API support without introducing a second provider identity: - `deepseek-v4-flash` and the GA `deepseek-v4-pro` use DeepSeek's Responses API. - Both models support opt-in native server-side `web_search` and stateless `web_search_call` replay. - Unknown/dated model IDs fail closed to Chat Completions until their capabilities are explicitly documented. - Responses support and native search remain separate capability flags in one central table. DeepSeek announced `deepseek-v4-pro` GA on 2026-08-13 (model version `DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813`). The current [Responses API guide](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/responses_api/) documents both V4 Flash and V4 Pro, function/native `web_search` tools, and replaying `web_search_call` items as-is. See also the [DeepSeek updates](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/updates/) and [thinking-mode guide](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/thinking_mode/). The implementation keeps the canonical `deepseek` provider, recomputes the wire protocol whenever the model changes, and only normalizes the official `api.deepseek.com` endpoint. Custom proxies are left alone. This builds on and supersedes #79103. Thanks to @hutao562 for the initial DeepSeek native-search exploration and one-for-one tool-swap approach. ## Related Issue Closes #80901 ## Type of Change - [ ] 🐛 Bug fix - [x] ✨ New feature - [ ] 🔒 Security fix - [x] 📝 Documentation update - [x] ✅ Tests - [ ] ♻️ Refactor ## Changes Made - Added a centralized, fail-closed DeepSeek capability table with independent `responses_api` and `native_web_search` flags; both exact GA V4 IDs are enabled. - Added model-aware routing across runtime resolution, credential pools/rotation, direct `AIAgent` construction, live and `/model` switches, and fallback activation. - Normalized only the official endpoint: - Responses: `https://api.deepseek.com` → SDK sends `/responses` - Chat Completions: `https://api.deepseek.com/v1` - custom proxies/lookalike/noncanonical URLs: unchanged - Added the `deepseek` web provider marker as explicit opt-in via `web.search_backend: deepseek`; a credential alone never auto-enables native search. - Replaced an already-enabled Hermes `web_search` function one-for-one with `{"type":"web_search"}`. Search is never granted additively, and Firecrawl/Tavily/etc. remain client-dispatched. - Captured, JSON-normalized, persisted, and replayed `web_search_call` items in original output order and preserved provider action/source data. - Preserved `web_search_call` through production Responses preflight on turn N+1. - Sanitized unsupported DeepSeek Responses fields after request overrides without regressing native compaction on other providers. - Normalized DeepSeek Responses reasoning levels to its documented wire values (`minimal→low`, `medium/xhigh→high`, `ultra→max`) and send `reasoning.effort: none` when thinking is disabled, since omission leaves DeepSeek thinking enabled by default. - Updated provider and web-search documentation for V4 Pro GA. ## How to Test Rebased onto current `main` at `edb33be51` and ran: ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \ tests/agent/transports \ tests/agent/test_codex_responses_adapter.py \ tests/cli/test_cli_provider_resolution.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_runtime_provider_resolution.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_model_switch_*.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_custom_provider_model_switch.py \ tests/hermes_cli/test_user_providers_model_switch.py \ tests/run_agent/test_credential_rotation_route_settings.py \ tests/run_agent/test_provider_fallback.py \ tests/run_agent/test_switch_model_pool_reload_52727.py \ tests/run_agent/test_run_agent_codex_responses.py \ tests/run_agent/test_native_compaction.py \ tests/run_agent/test_deepseek_responses_wire.py \ tests/run_agent/test_deepseek_reasoning_content_echo.py \ tests/plugins/model_providers/test_deepseek_profile.py \ tests/plugins/web/test_web_search_provider_plugins.py ``` Result: **658 passed**. Additional validation: - focused changed-path suite: **200 passed** - broader DeepSeek/Responses suite: **477 passed, 2 skipped** (the skips are credential-gated live tests) - Ruff: pass - `compileall`: pass - `git diff --check`: pass The local-wire E2E is parameterized over both V4 Flash and V4 Pro and uses the real OpenAI SDK against an in-process HTTP server. It verifies `/responses`, native tool serialization, default reasoning normalization, SSE parsing, field sanitization, production preflight, exact `web_search_call` preservation, and turn-N+1 replay without requiring a DeepSeek key. Authenticated live smoke testing against **both** `deepseek-v4-pro` and `deepseek-v4-flash` on 2026-08-14 passed through the production Hermes request builder and Responses transport. For each model, stale Chat Completions routing was corrected to `/responses`, native search produced `web_search_call` items plus a message, every call was replayed successfully on turn N+1, and a separate request with thinking disabled was accepted with `reasoning.effort: none`. Pro returned eight search calls and used 24,877 input tokens (18,176 cached) plus 1,164 output tokens, approximately **$0.004**. Flash returned two search calls and used 9,335 input tokens (4,224 cached) plus 364 output tokens, approximately **$0.00083**. The credential was loaded only into the test processes and was not logged or committed. ## Checklist - [x] Read contribution/repository guidance - [x] Conventional commits - [x] Changes are scoped to DeepSeek Responses/native search - [x] Added behavior and real-wire integration tests - [x] Updated documentation and provider descriptions - [x] Tested on macOS - [ ] Full `pytest tests/ -q` (broad affected-path suites above pass)
